# Skills Repo Git Hygiene: Worktree-Routed Edits and Explicit-Path Staging

The 2026-08-15 wrap-up of a multi-session effort on the `~/.claude/skills` git repo established several durable practices for working in a repository that is simultaneously a live configuration directory and a version-controlled artifact. Edits are routed through git worktrees because a background-isolation guard blocks direct edits to the shared checkout; the `.claude/` directory is excluded from commits by explicit-path staging and then permanently by `.gitignore`, because `.claude/worktrees/` holds four live git worktrees that would nest repositories if committed.

## Key Points

- **`.claude/worktrees/` must be gitignored.** It held four live git worktrees at the time of the session; committing it would nest repositories inside the repository. The exclusion was first achieved by explicit-path staging (deliberately naming every file to stage rather than using `git add -A`), then made permanent with a `.gitignore` line in commit `163db25`.
- **The background-isolation guard blocks direct edits to the shared checkout**, so skill edits route through a git worktree off `main` rather than being applied in place.
- **Commits shipped:** `faf6be8` (routing + description trims), `2c5a10a` (skill-authoring consolidation), `008f345` (doctor-plus, playwright-cli, presets gallery, 14 symlinks), `163db25` (`.gitignore`). `main` ended in sync with origin, working tree clean.
- **Pre-existing uncommitted work was committed only after diff review plus a credential scan** (private repo, clean) — four to five files that had been sitting in the working tree across sessions.
- **Two self-caught mistakes worth recording:** recommending removal of `anthropic-skills` (which would have destroyed portability), and a trim pass that silently dropped 20 trigger phrases while claiming it had not. The second was caught by the Codex review gate rather than by self-report.
- **Open lever on Codex exclusions:** dropping `mattpocock-skills` is the only remaining option for reducing Codex's 171 excluded skills (down from 187) — undecided.

## Details

The `~/.claude/skills` repository occupies an unusual position: it is the live configuration that the running agent reads from, and it is a git repository synced daily across machines. This dual role generates the hygiene requirements. Because it is live configuration, a background-isolation guard prevents direct writes to the shared checkout — an agent editing skills in place could alter the behavior of the very session performing the edit. Routing through a worktree off `main` isolates the edit until it is deliberately merged. Because it is a synced repository, deletions have cross-machine blast radius, which is why the [[concepts/browser-automation-stack-audit-mac]] remediation chose to neuter rather than delete two non-functional skills: the Windows machine may still have their dependencies.

The `.claude/worktrees/` problem is a specific instance of a general git hazard. Worktrees contain their own git metadata; committing a directory that holds four of them would embed repository state inside the tracked tree, producing the nested-repo confusion that git handles poorly and that is difficult to unwind after the fact. The two-step remedy is instructive: explicit-path staging solved it for the immediate commits (naming every intended file rather than relying on `git add -A` or `git add .`), and the `.gitignore` line made it structural so future sessions cannot reintroduce it by accident. Explicit-path staging generalizes as a discipline for any repository where the working tree contains a mixture of tracked source and live runtime state — the same class of caution as the [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] snapshotting, applied at the staging boundary rather than the destruction boundary. Committing the four-to-five pre-existing uncommitted files only after a diff review and a credential scan reflects the same posture: a private repo is not a reason to skip the scan, only a reason for the scan to be expected to come back clean.

The two self-caught mistakes are worth preserving because they illustrate different detection paths. The `anthropic-skills` removal recommendation was caught by reasoning — removing it would have destroyed the portability that the whole Codex/Claude Code effort was built to establish, so the consequence was visible before execution. The dropped trigger phrases were caught only by an external review gate, because the trimming pass's own account of its work was wrong: it reported preserving phrases it had in fact deleted. This is the same shape as the [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] pattern — an intermediate layer's self-report is not evidence — and it is the reason the outstanding batch trim of 36 over-ceiling skills described in [[concepts/skill-description-budget-ceiling]] needs diff-level verification rather than a completion claim.

# PP_Recruiting Workbook 012: Benchmark-Tagged Unified Grading

Workbook 012 of the PP_Recruiting project is workbook 010 plus a BENCHMARK tag and a new percentile-profile tab, completed and merged to `main` on 2026-09-26 (PR #2, merge commit `8a3de3a`). It changed no thresholds and no formulas; its purpose is to let per-position grading distributions be read off proven 2025 players. The workbook was staged for staff in `Send\`, and the session recorded three gotchas that must accompany it.

## Key Points

- **Benchmark files contained no new data.** All 710 top-2025 players were already present in the 2025 exports: 578 had zero eligibility remaining (the reason workbook 010 excluded them) and the remaining 132 were already 010 rows.
- **What 012 adds:** a BENCHMARK tag (PORTAL INPUT column BT, REVIEW BOARD column AL) and a final BENCHMARK PROFILES tab giving per-position 25th/median/75th percentiles plus share ≥75, computed live off REVIEW BOARD. Top End Speed is excluded pending mph confirmation. No thresholds or formulas were altered.
- **The data grades proven players low.** Of the 710 proven 2025 players, only 16% project AL or better, about half QS or better, and 78% still flag REVIEW — consistent with an earlier validation run. Mendoza is the exemplar: traits project FRP while a Player Impact of 98 trips REVIEW.
- **012's REVIEW count is inflated by ineligible players.** The displayed 2,352 REVIEW count drops to 010's 1,899 (1,708 with 150+ snaps) once the new Benchmark column is filtered to blank. The 011 screening-matrix numbers still refer to 010, and staff must be told this before opening 012.
- **012 is not loader-safe.** New data keeps loading onto 010, never 012 — the benchmark workbook is a read/analysis artifact, not the ingestion target.
- **Structural grading ceiling at OT/OG/C:** those positions carry only two traits each, so they can only land AA, QS, LIM, or NGE. This is a design consequence of the trait count, not a data defect.

## Details

The benchmark exercise began as an attempt to add proven-player reference data and ended by confirming that no new data existed to add — the value was entirely in tagging and summarizing rows already present. That result matters for interpretation: because the 578 zero-eligibility players were deliberately excluded from 010, tagging them back in for benchmark purposes reintroduces rows that the operational grading view intentionally omits. Hence the inflated REVIEW count and the blank-Benchmark filter that restores the operational numbers. The discipline adopted was to change nothing in the grading logic — no thresholds, no formulas — so that any difference between 010 and 012 is attributable solely to population, not to method. That is what makes the percentile profiles readable as a property of the players rather than of a revised rubric.

The substantive finding is that the grading system rates proven, productive 2025 players low: only 16% project AL or better and 78% still flag REVIEW. Mendoza makes the tension concrete — trait projections land at FRP while a Player Impact score of 98 nonetheless trips REVIEW, meaning the flag is firing on players whose production is close to the ceiling. Read together with the OT/OG/C two-trait ceiling, the pattern suggests the flagging thresholds and the trait coverage per position both need review before the REVIEW flag is treated as a screening signal. Two operational hazards were handled by file hygiene rather than documentation alone: workbook 012 was copied into `Send\` and the stale "Prototype - 003" workbook was moved to `_to_delete\`, so staff cannot open the wrong file. A STATUS correction (`a0cb038`) was pushed immediately after the merge because `main` still claimed 010 as latest, which would have hidden 010–012 from the Mac and from any fresh agent — the same cross-machine staleness problem that the machine-split closeout guards against.

Repository cleanup closed the branch: `worktree-fireflies-review-board-0915` was deleted locally and on GitHub, leaving a single-branch, clean repo. Git released the worktree cleanly, but Windows blocked deletion of the folder itself because Drive sync holds locks on `Desktop\DEV`; Eric cleared it manually, and this is expected on every worktree teardown on this laptop.

# Rounded Counts and Ratios in Always-Loaded Context Documents

On 2026-09-07 a config-hygiene pass corrected several drifted inventory counts in `~/DEV/CLAUDE.md` — 155 skills, 230 compiled articles, 849 notes, 38,832 of 56,707 files — and then changed the convention that had allowed them to drift. Exact figures were replaced with `~`-prefixed rounded values plus an inline note explaining why, and the Football-files row was rewritten from a raw pair of numbers into a ratio ("about two thirds of DEV") on the grounds that the proportion remains true as files accumulate while the absolute counts do not.

## Key Points

- **Four counts had drifted and two had not.** Skills, compiled articles, vault notes, and the file counts were corrected; the custom-CLI count (8) and the per-project `CLAUDE.md` count (18) were already accurate — slow-moving inventories drift more slowly.
- **Exact numbers in a long-lived context document go stale within weeks,** so the corrected values were deliberately rounded with `~` rather than restated precisely.
- **The rounding was documented in the file itself,** so a future reader (human or agent) does not "helpfully" restore precision and reintroduce the drift.
- **A ratio was substituted where one was available:** the Football-files row became "about two thirds of DEV," a statement that stays true as the denominator grows, unlike `38,832 of 56,707`.
- **Precision is a liability, not a virtue, when nothing recomputes it.** The value of an exact count is realized only at the moment of measurement; afterward it decays into a confident false claim.

## Details

The distinction the session drew is between numbers that are regenerated and numbers that are transcribed. A table built by a script from a data source can be exact because it is rebuilt whenever the source changes; a count typed into a context file is a snapshot with no refresh mechanism, and it begins decaying immediately. Writing `38,832 of 56,707` in such a file commits the document to a claim it cannot maintain, and — worse — the specificity signals to a reader that the figure was recently verified. Rounding to `~39,000` or restating as a proportion sacrifices nothing operationally useful, because no decision in this workspace depends on the fourth significant figure, while removing the false precision signal. This is the same asymmetry noted in [[concepts/interim-framing-for-open-data-collection]], where a figure's *status* mattered more than its accuracy, and the complement of [[concepts/generated-tables-versus-handwritten-prose-drift]], where authored prose drifted away from a generated table that had kept itself current.

The ratio substitution is the sharper move and deserves stating as a general preference: where a quantity can be expressed as a proportion of something that grows alongside it, the proportion is the more durable representation. "About two thirds of DEV is Football files" survives the addition of thousands of files on both sides of the fraction; "38,832 of 56,707" is falsified by the next sync. The transformation is not always available — a skill count has no natural denominator — but when it is, it converts a fact with a short half-life into one with a long one. Selecting the representation with the longest useful life is the design question, not merely getting today's number right.

The observation that two of six counts had not drifted is a useful secondary signal. The custom-CLI count and per-project `CLAUDE.md` count were still correct because those inventories change on a timescale of months, whereas skills, compiled knowledge articles, and vault notes all accumulate continuously. This suggests a triage rule for periodic hygiene passes: check the fast-moving inventories every time and the slow-moving ones rarely, rather than re-verifying every number at equal cost. The same session's `/claude-stack-doctor` run confirmed the rest of the stack healthy — `MEMORY.md` at 85% of cap (2,133/2,500 bytes, down from the over-cap condition three days earlier), a clean errors log, a backup with 31 targets, a verified cloud receipt, and all four repos synced.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature questi… [truncated]

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

## claude.ai Wispr Flow
Use this server when the user asks about meetings, notes, transcripts, or calendar information stored in Wispr Flow. For questions that may span multiple connected sources, use the relevant sources needed to answer the request. Read https://notes.wisprflow.ai/shared/ links with resolve_share_link rather than fetching the page. All timestamps returned by these tools are UTC (ISO 8601, ending in 'Z'). Before showing any time to the user, convert it to their local time zone — never present the raw UTC value.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. # Milvus Lite Version Skew Corrupts the memsearch Index

On 2026-10-10 the `daily-backup` job failed its `memsearch-index:full-set` step with the error "database was made by an older Milvus Lite version." Seventy-one other jobs completed; only the index step failed, and an independently running index process (pid 44870) ran ~29 minutes before exiting with the same error. The chosen remedy was to move `~/.memsearch/milvus.db` aside as `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10` and rebuild from scratch, on the grounds that the index is derived from markdown notes and therefore loses nothing. The rebuild indexed 14,614 chunks and exited 0.

## Key Points

- **The failure is version skew in a local database file, not corruption of source data.** A Milvus Lite upgrade left an on-disk database the new library refuses to open, and because the index is derived from markdown notes, discarding and rebuilding is the cheapest correct fix.
- **Move aside rather than delete.** The old database was renamed `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10`, keeping a rollback path and a dated record of what the pre-upgrade state was.
- **A rebuild must cover the full path set.** A partial path set is destructive — indexing a subset deletes previously indexed data. The full set is 13 paths, of which 12 exist (`~/.codex/memories` does not), and this constraint was already recorded in memory.
- **Two concurrent index runs contend for the same database lock,** so a duplicate run has to be stopped and the existing one allowed to finish; this is the same lock-contention signature previously seen as an exit-1 after a long wait.
- **The `dcg` guard blocked the agent's own `mv` of a path under `~`,** so the move had to be run by the user with a `!` prefix; separately, the guard blocked shell-variable redirects, and literal absolute paths in the memsearch invocation passed.
- **Verification is a positive log line, not the absence of an error:** confirm the next `daily-backup` run (or a hand run of `daily-backup.ps1`) shows the `INDEX full set` step passing before clearing `.errors.log`.

## Details

This is a textbook instance of install-time environment capture rotting: a library upgrade changed the reader while the written artifact stayed at the old format, and nothing surfaced until a scheduled job happened to touch it. What makes the diagnosis tractable is the derived/primary distinction — the Milvus database holds no information that does not exist in the markdown notes it was built from, so the decision tree collapses to "rebuild" rather than "migrate" or "recover." Recognizing that an artifact is regenerable is what licenses the destructive-looking move; the same reasoning that made interim publication cheap in the open-data case applies here to deleting four hours of indexing work. The rename rather than delete is still worth the keystrokes, because it costs nothing and preserves the ability to answer "what did the old file actually contain" if the rebuild turns out to have missed a path.

Two operational hazards surfaced around the rebuild rather than in it. The first is that the rebuild's correctness depends on its argument list: memsearch treats the supplied path set as authoritative, so indexing a subset silently drops everything outside it. That turns a convenient "just reindex the one folder that changed" into a data-loss operation, and it is why the full 13-path list (12 existing) was reconstructed from memory before the run. The second is lock contention. Two index processes against one database produce a stall whose externally visible form — a long wait, then a nonzero exit — is indistinguishable from a crash, which is exactly the signature previously catalogued for `memsearch-drain.ps1`. The correct first check on a long-running index is therefore "is another run already holding the lock," not "is the code broken."

The `dcg` guard's behavior is worth recording precisely because the session chose not to weaken it. The guard refuses any agent-issued `mv` of a path under the home directory and refuses shell-variable redirects, which meant the single necessary move had to be handed to the user as a `!`-prefixed command — the narrowest-sufficient escalation rather than a settings edit. Literal absolute paths inside the memsearch call were accepted, which is the workaround that kept the rebuild itself agent-runnable. No change was made to `settings.json`, keeping the guard intact for every subsequent session; this is the same posture taken when a dcg rule blocked branch deletion and a multi-repo status loop.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/memsearch-indexing-lock-docker-dependency]] — The prior lock-contention and Docker/Milvus dependency findings; this article adds the version-skew failure mode and the full-path-set constraint.
- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The accumulated catalogue of memsearch failure causes this extends.
- [[concepts/shutdown-induced-dlopen-failure-false-alarm]] — The complementary case where memsearch was never broken at all, making cause classification the first step.
- [[concepts/dcg-guard-false-positives-native-tool-workaround]] — The guard that blocked the `mv` and the shell-variable redirect, plus the escape hatches that worked.
- [[connections/narrowest-sufficient-escalation-over-blanket-bypass]] — Why a one-off `!` command was preferred over relaxing the guard in `settings.json`.
- [[connections/install-time-environment-capture-rots-silently]] — The general class: a host fact (library version) frozen at write time, detected only when something reads the artifact.
- [[concepts/clear-the-error-log-only-after-a-clean-run]] — Why `.errors.log` stays until the backup's `INDEX full set` line passes.
- [[connections/an-error-names-the-transport-not-the-cause]] — The rebuild log's connection timeouts naming a layer rather than a cause.

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-10-10.md]] — Backup-failure session (16:40): `memsearch-index:full-set` failing with "database was made by an older Milvus Lite version" while 71 jobs completed, pid 44870 running ~29 minutes to the same error, option 1 (move aside and rebuild) chosen on the grounds that the index is derived from markdown, `dcg` blocking Claude's `mv` and the user running `mv ~/.memsearch/milvus.db ~/.memsearch/milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10` directly. Hook-failure session (21:28): rebuild over 12 existing of 13 paths (`~/.codex/memories` absent), duplicate run pid 83951 stopped to avoid lock conflict, memory note that a partial path set deletes indexed data, 14,614 chunks indexed at exit 0 with connection timeouts in the log, no `settings.json` change, and verification specified as an `INDEX full set` pass in the backup log.

# Line-Ending Drift on Drive Download, Resolved by Stash Not Discard

On 2026-10-10 ten athlete files were pulled from Google Drive into the `SpecialRequests` repo's `Zinnecker_Skylar` folder. Every downloaded file registered as changed, but the difference was entirely line endings — Windows CRLF in the Drive copies against the Mac's committed LF — with no data change. The resolution was `git stash` rather than `git checkout --`, preserving the Drive copies while restoring the committed state, and the download script was given a permanent home at `~/.claude/scripts/sr-gws-fetch.py` plus a guard against overwriting existing files.

## Key Points

- **CRLF/LF drift makes a byte-identical-in-content download look like a full-file change.** The Drive copies originated on Windows; the committed copies are LF, so every line differs at the working-tree level while the semantic content is unchanged.
- **Stash, don't discard.** `git stash` keeps the downloaded Drive copies recoverable while restoring the GitHub state, where a discard would have destroyed the only local record of what Drive actually held.
- **A size-based download check can silently overwrite across a line-ending boundary.** Because CRLF and LF versions of the same file differ in byte size, a "skip if same size" heuristic does not skip — it re-downloads and overwrites. The fix was an explicit never-overwrite-existing-files guard.
- **The ad-hoc fetch script was promoted to `~/.claude/scripts/sr-gws-fetch.py`,** turning a one-off into a durable, reusable tool rather than leaving it in a scratch location.
- **A submodule scare resolved as a non-issue:** `Wilhelm_Brody_RTP` was confirmed intact on the Mac with no missing git folder.

## Details

The underlying hazard is that a working-tree diff reports on the representation, not the content, and on a cross-platform repo the representation is the thing that differs. This is the same mechanism that produced phantom conflicts and phantom diffs in earlier cross-machine sessions, and it recurs here through a new route — a cloud download rather than a git operation. The practical consequence is that the usual reflex on seeing ten changed files ("revert them, the download went wrong") is wrong in both directions: the download did not go wrong, and reverting would discard the one copy that proves it. Choosing `git stash` keeps both states addressable and defers the decision, which is the right move when the artifact's correct disposition is not yet established.

The size-check defect deserves recording as a design lesson about guard predicates. "Skip the download if the local file is already the same size" is a reasonable-sounding idempotency check that happens to be coupled to exactly the property line-ending conversion changes, so the guard reliably fires in the one case where it should not. The replacement — never overwrite an existing file at all — is coupled to a property the conversion cannot affect, which is why it holds. This is the same failure shape as a guard checking writability where readability was needed: the predicate was adjacent to the intent rather than identical to it, so it reported a clean decision while doing the wrong thing. Promoting the script to `~/.claude/scripts/` is the complementary move, since a guard written into a scratch script protects only the run it was written for.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/dev-sync-encoding-mangling-phantom-conflicts]] — The prior instance where a Windows save mangled encoding and produced ~200 phantom conflicts in the same cross-machine repo set.
- [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]] — Where 26 of 36 cross-machine conflicts turned out to be CRLF-only, establishing this as the dominant false-conflict class.
- [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] — The `autocrlf` mechanism and `git update-index --refresh` as the non-destructive way to clear CRLF phantom diffs.
- [[connections/preconditions-that-check-the-wrong-thing]] — The size-check guard coupled to the wrong property, reporting a clean skip decision while overwriting.
- [[connections/ground-truth-checks-must-match-the-lying-layer]] — Why a working-tree comparison is the wrong instrument when the working tree is the transforming layer.
- [[connections/classify-the-conflict-by-the-artifacts-kind]] — The discard-vs-merge-vs-dedupe taxonomy that makes "stash and decide later" the safe default.
- [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] — The general preference for a recoverable snapshot before any destructive git operation.

# Two Sessions Drafted the Same Batch: Check Master Before Running a Backlog

On 2026-10-10 two concurrent Claude sessions independently worked Batch 100 (questions Q01–Q96) of the sports-science research-library pipeline. One session completed the full audit-validate-assemble cycle and merged it as PR #25 (IDs 1788–1863); the other had drafted 64 of 96 papers before discovering the merge, at which point it halted. The 64 drafts were kept in a temp folder as a record only and explicitly not merged, and the next batch was re-anchored to start at ID 1864.

## Key Points

- **The shared backlog provided no mutual exclusion.** Both sessions picked the same next-unprocessed range because nothing in the repo marked the range as claimed, and the duplication was only visible after one side merged.
- **The stop decision was to discard, not reconcile.** Rather than diffing 64 duplicate drafts against the merged set, the drafts were left in place as a record and the next pick moved forward to ID 1864 — cheaper than adjudicating two independent derivations of the same work.
- **The recorded rule is to check master before starting a batch,** and to confirm the other session has actually finished before restarting rather than inferring it from a merge.
- **Batch numbering collided independently.** Batch 99 had already consumed numbers 99–106, so Batch 100's output files were renumbered 107–114; the collision was caught before the file write by checking existing batches at assembly time.
- **Assembly failed twice on a missing field before succeeding:** inputs lacked `pilotDomain`, and then 14 EXCLUDE records carried no domain at all, since draft/verify stages do not assign one to excluded records. The fallback was to file all 14 under Sports Medicine & Injury, the batch's largest domain.
- **Duplicate-DOI detection worked within the batch:** Q04 and Q05 were the same article, so Q05 was set EXCLUDE with its reason pointing at Q04's assigned ID (1804).

## Details

The duplication is a scheduling failure rather than a tooling failure, and it is the second recorded instance of concurrent sessions colliding on the same repositories. The distinguishing feature here is that the collision was invisible until completion: both sessions could read the repo, both could see the same unprocessed range, and neither wrote anything that would warn the other off. A backlog consumed by multiple workers needs either a claim marker or a pre-flight read of the merged state, and the session chose the latter as the standing rule because it requires no new mechanism — read master, see what IDs exist, start after them. The deeper principle is that shared state changes between the moment an instruction is formed and the moment it is acted on, so a session resuming a long-running pipeline must re-derive its starting point rather than trust a remembered one.

The assembly failures carry a separate, transferable lesson about which records a pipeline stage is responsible for. Domain assignment happened only for records that survived to verification, so EXCLUDE records arrived at assembly with an empty field that the assembler required — a gap that only manifests on batches containing exclusions. Filing the 14 under the batch's largest domain is a pragmatic fallback rather than a correct classification, and it should be read as a hole in the schema: either the draft stage should assign a provisional domain, or the assembler should accept unassigned excludes. The batch-number collision has the same shape at the filename layer, where the fix was checking existing batch numbers before writing rather than trusting the batch's own label.

The session also produced a list of papers whose extracted content conflicts internally and needs human adjudication: Q60 (sample is coaching staff, not athletes), Q64 (risk ratio disagrees with Table 1), Q67 (confidence interval differs between abstract and Results), Q72 (extraction count mismatch), Q66 (Current Opinion piece framed as a narrative review, and ultimately flipped INCLUDE→EXCLUDE), Q37 (non-athlete sample), Q34 (r² conflict), plus Q13, Q14, Q16, Q38, and Q94 queued for spot checks. These are abstract-versus-body disagreements inside single sources, the same class of defect that makes a verified citation no guarantee of the claim built on it. The library ended at 1,831 rows with 82 PDFs remaining in the backlog.

- [[concepts/concurrent-session-repo-state-reread]] — The direct precedent: a merge performed by a concurrent session discovered only after the fact.
- [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]] — The predecessor batch-import campaign with the same round/ID-block structure and the same citation-verification hazards.
- [[connections/real-citations-do-not-validate-claims]] — The flagged internal conflicts (RR, CI, r², sample population) as failures of extraction fidelity and inferential license rather than source existence.

# Suspending a Pipeline at a Rate Limit With Drafts Already Cached

On 2026-10-10 a batch of twelve parallel Opus audit groups hit an account session limit: group 8 completed (Q57–Q64 verified), group 12 managed one call, and groups 1–7 and 9–12 failed outright, with the limit resetting at 2:20 PM Central. Because all 96 drafts (Q01–Q96) had already been written to `~/Library/Caches/sportsci-batch-100` before the audit stage ran, the correct response was to suspend work until reset and re-run only the failed audit groups — no re-drafting required.

## Key Points

- **Writing the expensive intermediate to disk before the next stage makes a rate-limit wall cheap.** The drafts survived the failure, so the retry cost was only the failed audits, not the whole pipeline.
- **Parallel audit groups consume quota disproportionately fast.** Twelve concurrent Opus calls exhausted the session limit before most groups finished a single call, so fan-out trades wall-clock time for a much higher chance of hitting the ceiling mid-run.
- **The decision was to wait for reset rather than close out mid-pipeline.** With the batch drafted but unaudited, closeout would have recorded an artifact in an unverifiable state; the reset time was known, which makes waiting a bounded cost.
- **Per-group outcomes must be tracked individually,** because completion is ragged — group 8 finished, group 12 partially ran, and ten groups did not start, so "re-run the audits" is only actionable against a per-group record.
- **A session-limit failure is a quota signal, not a defect,** and is distinguishable from a code failure only by the error text.

## Details

The structural lesson is about where to place the durable boundary in a multi-stage pipeline. Drafting is the expensive, token-heavy stage; auditing is the one most likely to fan out across parallel calls and therefore the one most likely to hit a ceiling. Writing drafts to a cache directory before auditing begins means the quota wall lands on the cheap-to-retry side of the boundary, and the explicit note that the cache made retry safe "without re-drafting" is the payoff. The same reasoning appears in the shutdown case — write the durable artifact first so that a reaped process degrades the result rather than erasing it — and generalizes to any stage sequence where one stage is materially more expensive than the next.

The fan-out observation is the counterweight to the usual case for parallelism. Twelve simultaneous Opus audit groups maximizes throughput only if the quota holds; if it does not, the failure is distributed across ten groups rather than concentrated in one, and the bookkeeping burden of resuming is correspondingly larger. The practical consequence is that group size should be chosen against the remaining quota rather than against available concurrency, which is the same batch-size-controls-yield-not-just-speed finding recorded for the Gemini-metered extraction runs. The decision to wait rather than work around is also notable: where the blocked resource had a manual substitute, prior sessions proceeded by hand; here the blocked resource was the model itself, with no substitute, so stopping at a known-good state with a written resume path was the only correct move.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/quota-metered-pipeline-execution-strategy]] — The checkpoint-every-N and batch-size-controls-yield findings this instance reproduces at a different provider.
- [[connections/reviewer-unavailability-as-a-forcing-function]] — The substitutable-versus-not distinction that makes waiting correct here and working around correct elsewhere.

# Registry Drift: 14 Items, Folders Without Rows and Rows Without Folders

A 2026-10-10 closeout pass found the project registry misaligned on 14 items, drifting in both directions at once: folders present on disk with no registry row, and registry rows pointing at folders that no longer exist. Reconciliation was deferred to a later pass rather than attempted during closeout. The same pass flagged three projects (`NCAA_BestPractices_Doc`, `HPI_Protocol`, `Education_Curriculum`) as tripping the 7-day staleness rule and needing one step each, and left two decisions explicitly unassigned.

## Key Points

- **The drift is bidirectional, which means neither direction can be the authority.** A folder with no row and a row with no folder require opposite fixes — add an entry versus remove or re-point one — so the reconciliation cannot be a one-way sync.
- **Fourteen misaligned items were recorded rather than fixed,** keeping the closeout scoped to reporting and leaving the reconciliation for a dedicated pass.
- **The 7-day staleness rule fired on three projects** needing one step each, which converts "these are cold" into a concrete minimum action per project.
- **Two decisions were left named and unassigned:** whether to revive `WomensHealth_Survey` (recommendation recorded as yes, flagged for Eric) and who receives the TOS one-pager and case review.
- **A recommendation plus an explicit flag is a complete closeout output** for a decision the session cannot make — the alternative, acting on the recommendation, would substitute the agent's judgment for the owner's.

## Details

Bidirectional drift is the diagnostic detail that determines the shape of the fix. A registry that is merely incomplete can be repaired by discovery — walk the disk, add what is missing — and a registry that is merely stale can be repaired by pruning. When both failures are present, the registry and the filesystem have each accumulated entries the other does not know about, and reconciliation requires a per-item judgment about which side is right. That is precisely why classification cannot be inferred from names and why ambiguous candidates have never been auto-promoted in this registry: the cheap list is a work queue, not an answer. Recording the count and deferring is therefore the honest closeout output, because a bulk auto-fix in either direction would have silently destroyed correct entries.

The decision handling is the transferable part. Both open items — reviving a paused survey project and naming a recipient for a finished one-pager — are owner decisions, and the session's output for each is a recommendation plus a flag rather than an action. This mirrors the deliberate hold placed on finished-looking deliverables elsewhere: the artifact is ready, the release condition is stated, and the condition is a human's to satisfy. It also matches the closeout discipline of reporting drift without fixing it, and of reporting items this session did not own. The 7-day rule's output has the same character but is more actionable: rather than labeling three projects stale, it specifies that each needs one step, which is a bar low enough to clear and specific enough to verify.

# Connection: Put the Durable Boundary Before the Stage Most Likely to Fail

## The Connection

Three independent 2026-10-10 failures were each survivable for the same structural reason: in every case a durable copy existed on the cheap side of the boundary where the failure landed. Ninety-six research drafts had been written to a cache directory before the audit stage hit an account session limit, so the retry cost was the audits alone. The memsearch Milvus database was discardable because it is derived from markdown notes that were never at risk, making "rebuild from scratch" a complete fix. Ten Drive-downloaded athlete files were preserved by `git stash` rather than discarded, so the only local record of what Drive held survived the revert.

## Key Insight

Resilience in these pipelines came not from making any stage more reliable but from choosing where the recoverable copy sits relative to the stage that fails. The useful question when designing a multi-stage run is not "what might break" but "if the next stage fails, what will I have to redo" — and the answer is set by whether the prior stage's output was materialized.

The three cases show the boundary being placed by three different mechanisms, which is what makes the pattern worth naming. The draft cache was *deliberate*: the pipeline writes its expensive intermediate to disk before fanning out across parallel model calls, exactly the stage most likely to hit a ceiling. The Milvus rebuild was *inherent*: because the index is derived, the boundary exists whether anyone designs it or not, and the real work was recognizing the artifact's derived status so that deleting it became obviously safe rather than frightening. The stash was *reactive*: the boundary was created at the moment of the revert by someone who noticed that discard and restore are not the same operation.

The corollary is that the cost of a failure is often decided long before the failure. Writing drafts to a cache costs almost nothing when things go well and converts a quota wall from a total loss into a partial one; the same ordering logic appears in the rule that a session-end hook should write its durable artifact first so a reaped job degrades rather than erases. Conversely, when the boundary is absent, an ordinary failure becomes unrecoverable — which is why an archive step that overwrote its own target, or a trim of a memory line with only one copy, were far more dangerous than the operations that triggered them.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-10 (16:41): "Drafts saved to cache before audits; safe to retry without re-drafting" — all 96 drafts in `~/Library/Caches/sportsci-batch-100` while audit groups 1–7 and 9–12 failed on the session limit.
- 2026-10-10 (16:40): "Chose option 1: move the corrupted index database aside and rebuild it from scratch. The index data is derived from markdown notes, so nothing is lost."
- 2026-10-10 (12:36): "Stash, don't discard: preserved Drive copies while restoring GitHub state."
- 2026-10-10 (16:40): the old database renamed to `milvus.db.pre-3x-2026-10-10` rather than deleted, creating a dated rollback point alongside the rebuild.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/rate-limit-suspension-with-cached-drafts]] — The deliberate case: the cache placed before the fan-out stage.
- [[concepts/milvus-lite-version-upgrade-breaks-index]] — The inherent case: a derived artifact that is always safe to rebuild.
- [[concepts/line-ending-drift-on-drive-download]] — The reactive case: a boundary created at the moment of the revert.
- [[concepts/session-end-hooks-run-during-shutdown]] — The same ordering rule stated for the shutdown window: durable artifact first, so a reaped job degrades.
- [[concepts/pre-destructive-git-backup-discipline]] — Per-step snapshots as the deliberate form of this boundary before destructive git operations.
- [[connections/the-preservation-step-must-itself-be-verified]] — The inverse: when the boundary itself is broken, the safety net is worse than none.
- [[concepts/never-trim-a-memory-line-without-checking-for-a-second-copy]] — The cost when no second copy exists on the far side of the operation.

entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
